title: George Morrison: Anishinaabe Expressionist Artist
abstract: George MorrisonAnishinaabe Expressionist Artist Gerald Vizenor (bio) George Morrison was an eminent expressionist painter with a singular romantic vision and an erudite sense of natural reason and liberty. He created an elusive shimmer of "endless space," the color and eternal motion of nature. The horizons he painted were inspired by nature and lightened by his watch and visual memories of Lake Superior near the Grand Portage Reservation in Minnesota. The artistic creations of George Morrison and Allan Houser were presented in the recent inaugural exhibition of the Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian (NMAI). "Morrison and Houser belonged to a small disparate group of Native American artists," noted Truman Lowe in Native Modernism, "who ushered in a new, modernist era in Native art history, in which identification with a uniform Indian aesthetic gave way to greater freedom for personal experimentation and expression."1 Morrison was an artist of modern Native liberty. Native American Indian artists clearly demonstrated the sentiments of romanticism and modernism many generations before occidental dominance, but the name and notion of personal, emotive creative practices that departed from selected traditions have been embraced only recently. Native artists were expressionists and modernists by continental barter, tricky conversions, innovations, transformation, natural reason, survivance, and by nature; these modernist Native visions and mien were brushed aside as simulations of Native "traditions" were constructed by social scientists, museum curators, institutions, and agencies of the federal government. Modernism and the sentiments of chance, personal visions, and imagic transformations in art were Native practices and much more widespread [End Page 646] than the elite wend of occidental entitlements would sanction in the discovery of Native art, production, and commerce. George Morrison was a Native modernist painter, and his inspiration was both innate, Native by sentiments of natural reason and memory, and learned by art history, museums, and galleries. He was roused more by the imagic traces of nature, motion, color, and abstract patterns than he was by the academies of modernist turns, modes, and representations. Morrison, in other words, was a Native romanticist and modernist and an eminent expressionist painter by any cultural measure. Horizon Lines Morrison told Margot Fontunato Galt in Turning the Feather Around that the "basis of all art is nature." The North Shore of Lake Superior "was subconsciously in my psyche, prompting some of my images."2 Morrison was nurtured in the presence of indigenous sounds and light created by the seasons of the lake. He conceived of these images in the abstract rush of colors and memory, not by naturalism or the mere academic representations of the natural world. Clearly he perceived that nature was never silence but rather a brace of colors and the constancy of sound, a natural music. Anishinaabe lexicons have no specific name or word for romanticism, no traditional condition, distinction, mode, or practice that separates natural reason from creation. Natives practiced a natural art that anticipated the party of romanticism and modernism by emotive, personal, creative expressions in stories, images, and objects of wood, bone, hide, bark, and stone. Reason was inspired by nature, and Native artists created stories and images of singular visions, a distinctive and eccentric individuality. Anishinaabe woodland artists were aesthetic by natural reason—emotive romanticists, expressionists, and surrealists in a time of continental liberty. Surely Natives perceived artistic expression as more than mere resistance to realism, naturalism, and other occidental varieties of artistic production and historical movements. The Anishinaabe word mazinaadin, an animate, transitive verb, means to "make an image," and the word aakwendam, an animate, intransitive verb, means "feelings" and "intense desires" in translation. These two words provide a sense of the emotive creation of an image and imply [End Page 647] the artistic conditions of romanticism but not the movement or reaction to tradition or neoclassicism. Other words related to mazinaadin, a transitive image or imagic motion, are names of new experiences. The word mazinaatese, for instance, means "movie," and mazinaakide means "pictured" or "photographed." Similarly, the emotive word aakwaadiz means "fierce" in the language of the Anishinaabe. Morrison was inspired by expressionism, an art movement already underway at the time of his birth, September 30, 1919, in Chippewa City, Minnesota, a Native village located...

title: When Satire More Than Closed on Saturday Night: Henry Fielding and the Licensing Act of 1737
abstract: When Satire More Than Closed on Saturday Night Henry Fielding and the Licensing Act of 1737 Steven Dedalus Burch George S. Kaufman once famously defined satire as what closed Saturday night. This comment renders satire, among other comedic forms, to be uncommercial, not ready to support the weight and economic obligation of a mainstream comedy. Besides, satires become dated and irrelevant very quickly—hence, the warning to would-be producers and authors. In eighteenth-century England, however , Henry Fielding wrote satires that closed not only Saturday night but virtually everything within the London theatre. In the 1730s, after some false starts, Fielding began to find his mature voice as a playwright, through literary burlesque and, only later, political satire. Burlesque, defined as an exaggerated parody of a literary form or style, had been around since the ancient Greek theatre of Aristophanes , especially his parodies of Euripides. (Women Celebrating the Thesmophoria [411 BCE] and The Frogs [405 BCE] are among the earliest burlesques.) Fielding began his career with a succession of burlesques on such topics as Shakespeare and heroic tragedy, neoclassicism, Italian opera, and Colley Cibber with such audience favorites as The Tragedy of Tragedies; or, The Life and Death of Tom Thumb the Great (1731), The Welsh Opera (1731), and Covent-Garden Tragedy (1732) and within a few short years could claim to be the most popular playwright in London.1 These burlesques opened up in Fielding a channel for his anger at the banal, pretentious writing and musical fads of the day. But, more important , they were to provide him with a platform for his political revulsion at the open corruption of the court of George II, his chief minister Robert Walpole, and the Parliament. Robert Walpole, who had become Fielding’s chief opponent and sa- 76 S T E V E N D E D A L U S B U R C H tirical target, had become the first Lord of the Treasury and Chancellor of the Exchequer under George I, a position he maintained when George II ascended to the throne. He quickly became the king’s favorite and, subsequently, the most powerful and influential of the king’s ministers. In point of fact, most historians date the birth of the modern British prime minister to Walpole’s administration. Throughout his ministry, which lasted more than two decades, Walpole exercised extraordinary cunning in his manipulation of the House of Commons, exerting a profound influence on the structure of eighteenth -century politics. But that cunning was seriously undermined by his open and blatant use of patronage and even outright bribery in maintaining his political power. His opposition included many writers of the day, and several, including Fielding, wrote for the opposition newspaper, The Craftsman. These writers scathingly lampooned Walpole’s ministry in pamphlets, ballads, and newspapers, helping to bring about a complete and utter contempt by the public toward Parliament and politics. In 1736 Fielding wrote a five-act masterpiece of inspired, sustained comic invective, Pasquin, and it was a box-office and critical sensation. So much so that Fielding was encouraged to pursue a newer, looser form of writing, merging the literary burlesque he had recently mastered, especially in The Tragedy of Tragedies, with a scattershot satirical approach to the politics and culture of England. Sadly, the result of Fielding’s growth as a dramatist helped to bring about the Licensing Act of 1737, which abruptly terminated his career in the theatre. The effects of the Licensing Act have been well documented and will only be summarized here. Leading up to that summary, this essay will look at three of Fielding ’s last plays, beginning with Pasquin (1736) and then turning to The Historical Register of 1736 and Eurydice Hiss’d (both 1737) and examine how Fielding blends burlesque with topical satire in addition to breaking new ground in the drama.2 Pasquin Pasquin is a rehearsal play of the type established by George Villiers in his The Rehearsal (1671). title: Tragic Modernities by Meriam Leonard, and: Adorno and Modern Theatre: The Drama of the Damanged Self in Bond, Rudkin, Barker, and Kane by Karoline Gritzner
abstract: Reviewed by: Tragic Modernities by Meriam Leonard, and: Adorno and Modern Theatre: The Drama of the Damanged Self in Bond, Rudkin, Barker, and Kane by Karoline Gritzner David Krasner Tragic Modernities. By Meriam Leonard. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 2015; pp. 224. Adorno and Modern Theatre: The Drama of the Damanged Self in Bond, Rudkin, Barker, and Kane. By Karoline Gritzner. Basingstoke, UK: Palgrave Macmillan, 2015, pp. 206. Tragedy and modernity have had a contested relationship in critical theory. They divide on the one side along the lines of classicism (Aristotle) and neoclassicism as "pure" tragedy, and on the other Romanticism, eventuating into modern realism and the avant-garde, as the root of modernity. Two works in particular, George Steiner's The Death of Tragedy and Raymond Williams's Modern Tragedy, both written in the 1960s, lay the groundwork in considering their combination (or lack thereof): Steiner posits an incompatibility between tragedy and modernity, whereas Williams postulates a mutuality via modern alienation. The books under review here add considerably to the debate, with both largely supporting Williams over Steiner, asserting that modernity serves as fecund ground through which tragedy reconfigures and amplifies its aesthetic accountability. Meriam Leonard's Tragic Modernities contends that German idealism's emphasis on tragedy (primarily Schelling, Hegel, and Hölderlin) initiates modern tragedy by situating the tragic in the conflict between individual freedom and collective necessity. The German idealist concept of tragedy "inaugurates the entry of tragedy into modern thought" (5), Leonard argues, by demonstrating "not just how tragedy has shaped modern political discourse, but also how the political debates of modernity can offer important insight into tragic theatre" (10). Similarly, Karoline Gritzner's Adorno and Modern Theatre uses Adorno as the template to examine modern political thought and human suffering through tragic representation, where Adorno, while supporting art generally, calls into question modern aesthetic experience as, in Gritzner's words, an "anathema in the discourse of the culture industry" (4). Leonard examines tragedy in light of revolution, metaphysics, history, gender, and subjectivity. Modern tragedy, she says in her first chapter, draws from Marxism the "functioning in a modern world that includes revolution and the oppressive social structures that necessitate it" (38). In this way, Leonard challenges the left-wing dismissal of tragedy for its alleged anti-revolutionary "quietism and irrationalist nihilism" (40); instead (building on Raymond Williams), "tragedy both describes the conditions of alienation that make revolution desirable and critiques the willful blindness of revolutions that fail to acknowledge the persistence of human suffering in their midst" (ibid.). "Tragedy and Metaphysics," examines the freedom verses necessity conflict essential to Hegel, Schelling, and Hölderlin. Taking as a starting point Das älteste Systemprogramm des deutschen Idealismus (The Oldest Program for a System of German Idealism [1796], also called the System-Programme and likely written by the three idealists), this fragmentary text, influenced by Kant, posits a merger of philosophy, ethics, and poetry. Kant divided reason, ethics, and aesthetics into three separate entities (Critiques); the idealists embraced Kant's themes, but denied parsing, arguing instead for a synergistic and unifying alliance of the concepts. The German idealists, writes Leonard, called for a "new mythology," one that rejects the tripartite arrangements "that arise from Kant's critical system with a plea for a return to antiquity. Where the legacy of Kantian thought had left nature in conflict with reason, philosophy at odds with art, and the populace distanced from the thinkers" (47), the System-Programme and its followers called for a return to Hellenism and the appropriation of its unifying aesthetics. "Tragedy and History" centers on Carl Schmitt, an unrepentant Nazi sympathizer, whose 1956 book Hamlet or Hecuba: The Intrusion of Time into the Play examines the relationship of tragedy and history. In her effort to validate though not redeem Schmitt, Leonard calls attention to his similarities with liberal philosophers (Adorno and Benjamin) by locating Schmitt's emphasis on myth as a coadunate with history. For Schmitt, she writes, "myth does not stand opposed to history but rather represents a shared knowledge that is comparable to the common experience of historical actuality" (87). title: Virginia By Design: The Making of Tuckahoe and the Remaking of Monticello
abstract: Virginia By Design: The Making of Tuckahoe and the Remaking of Monticello CAMILLE WELLS In their discussions of Thomas Jefferson's second Monticello, scholars have privileged his thoughtful and inventive restatements ofEuropean neoclassicism-particularly of those academic forms and motifs with which he became acquainted during his ministry in France. This approach to whatJefferson famously called his "essay in architecture" is fair and useful as far as it goes.1 Monticello, however, was so physically complex, so long in the making, and so manifestly Jefferson's evolving attempt to reconcile a host of architectural functions and meanings, that it has many more stories to tell (fig. 1). One of those stories concernsJefferson's sustained allegiance, his own protestations notwithstanding, to the conventions ofVirginia house planning as they had crystallized by about 1750.2 Embedded in this story is Jefferson's long and intimate association with Tuckahoe, a genteel colonial Virginia house that incorporates many of the characteristics for which he professed disapproval, but which nevertheless became the basis for the plan and social organization of his second Monticello. His descendants often said that ThomasJefferson's earliest memory was of a trip made on horseback, cushioned on a pillow and secure in the arms of a trusted slave. The journey was formidable for a child of two or three: from Shadwell, the Albemarle County plantation where his parents had settled and-where he had been born, to Tuckahoe, one of the many Randolph family plantations that sprawled along both banks of theJames River.3 This trip eastward into Goochland County was occasioned by an unusual request made by William Randolph. First cousin ofJane Randolph Jefferson and fast friend of Peter Jefferson, the ailing William Randolph had in the summer of 1745 turned fretful thoughts to the impending orphanhood of his three small children. Having already established, in a will composed shortly after his wife's death in 1742, that his son "shall not be educated att the Colledge of vVilliam and Mary in Virginia nor sent to England on any account 44 ARrus whatever" but should be instructed entirely by private tutors, Randolph specified the means by which this directive should come to pass. In a codicil he wrote: Whereas I have appointed by my will that my dear only son Thomas Mann Randolph should have a private education given him in my house at Tuckahoe, my will is that my dear and loving friend Mr. PeterJefferson do move down with his family to my Tuckahoe house and remain there till my son comes of age with whom my dear son & his [two older] sisters shall live.4 PeterJefferson did indeed moveJaneJefferson and their own three children to Tuckahoe sometime late in 1745 or early in 1746.5 How long they remained in residence there is not clear. PeterJefferson's accounts show careful oversight ofTuckahoe's agricultural production through 1755, but during these years he also was engaged in arduous surveying expeditions for the colony of Virginia.6 Thus he often was away from Tuckahoe, where appointed managers-and perhaps also his wifesaw to the everyday business of plantation life. Peter Jefferson had resumed residence at Shadwell by 1754, the year he attained the positions of county surveyor, lieutenant of the county militia, and county representative in the General Assembly.7 His records indicate continuing oversight of Tuckahoe affairs, however, and among these were fees paid to the Reverend William Douglas of St. James-Northam Parish in Goochland County for schooling his son. Thus young Thomas, if not his mother and sisters, remained among Randolph cousins at Tuckahoe until his father's untimely death in 1757.8 The boy was then fourteen years old. Modern historians and memorialists of Thomas Jefferson honor Tuckahoe as the site of his earliest education -or as the Commonwealth Chapter of the Daughters of the American Revolution stated on a small plaque Fig. 1. i\1onticello, Albemarle County, Virginia. Begun in 1771 and completed in about 1809. (Holsinger Studio Collection, Albert H. Small Special Collections Library, University ofVirginia) erected near the house, "[H] ere the discipline of his noble mind began." Tuckahoe thereafter vanishes from most chronicles of Jefferson's eventful and illustrious life story. Jefferson himself...

title: Christopher Wheeldon, Between Ballet's Past and Future
abstract: Christopher Wheeldon, Between Ballet's Past and Future Jay Rogoff (bio) Christopher Wheeldon's early ballets made him a sensation. They had wit and sparkle, and while they suggested both his Royal Ballet experience with Frederick Ashton-style feeling and his New York City Ballet training in George Balanchine's neoclassicism, they looked neither derivative nor like apprentice works. He knew how to move groups of dancers expressively, whether setting ballet students to mirroring each other at the barre in his Scènes de Ballets (1999), or angling a file of men through ranks of women in Mercurial Manoeuvres (2000). He could devise large-scale comic entertainments with ingenious designs, such as Scènes, in which the barre diagonally split Ian Falconer's set into a fin-de-siècle Russian dance studio and its mirror image, or the backstage ballet farce, Variations Sérieuses (2001), for which Falconer conjured a sidelong view of a ballet from the wings. He could spin a narrative, turning his 2003 collaboration with actor John Lithgow, Saint-Saëns's Carnival of the Animals, into a suite of splashy beast dances performed for a child locked overnight in a natural history museum, and in The Nightingale and the Rose (2007), creating a strutting and twittering bird-role for NYCB's Wendy Whelan to rival ballet's swans and firebirds. Wheeldon also experimented with ballet's classic expression of sexual engagement, the pas de deux, and while romantic transport seems not his taste, he made these encounters absorbing, some of them incorporating jokes like quirkily angled legs and arms, others exploring ingenious (sometimes overly ingenious) methods of partnering, and still others introducing soaring, figure-skating displays, like the man's lifting the woman horizontally overhead in the much-loved After the Rain (2005).Finally, he discovered in the piano and chamber music of György Ligeti a previously unmined vein of rhythmically varied, spiky, and attractively discordant scores that, in ballets like Polyphonia (2001) and Morphoses and Continuum (both 2002), let Wheeldon's choreography grow stunningly modern. At the time it looked as though Ligeti, whose music Wheeldon now unfortunately seems to have abandoned, might continue to inspire his choreography as Stravinsky had Balanchine's. Early in the new millennium, dance writers almost unanimously praised Wheeldon—and rightly—as the best thing to happen to ballet during the period after Balanchine's death twenty years before. He had [End Page 280] quit dancing in 2000, still in his twenties and a rising NYCB soloist, to choreograph full-time, and in 2006 he announced he would found his own company and not seek reappointment to his post as NYCB's Resident Choreographer. During its first two years, his awkwardly named Morphoses/The Wheeldon Company hired American and European stars to perform his own works and those of other young choreographers, almost always to live music. Watching NYCB's Ashley Bouder, Gonzalo Garcia, Maria Kowroski, and Wendy Whelan; the Royal Ballet's Leanne Benjamin, Darcey Bussell, Alina Cojocaru, and Edward Watson; and other major companies' principals perform together made those first seasons exciting. Wheeldon planned for a permanent company within a few years, based in New York but offering an annual London season, while also touring extensively to spread its gospel. That gospel includes Morphoses's commitment to artistic collaboration. While the company mainly dances Wheeldon works, Wheeldon not only stages others' ballets but also commissions new ones, occasionally with new music, and usually with new stage décor by contemporary fine artists rather than theater designers. He has spoken often of his admiration for the way Serge Diaghilev convened major choreographers (Balanchine, Fokine, Nijinska, Nijinsky), composers (Milhaud, Prokofiev, Ravel, Stravinsky), and artists (Braque, Dali, Matisse, Picasso) to collaborate for his Ballets Russes. Despite a budget less than one-third the size of what he had hoped for at this point in the company's young life, the economic recession has not diminished Wheeldon's ambitions. Whereas financial necessity helped Balanchine commit to stripping away expensive costumes and scenery to let ballet stand alone with its music as a modern art, Wheeldon persists in his pursuit of the Gesamtkunstwerk and economizes elsewhere: he still has no permanent...

title: Art of Life Now : Theatrical Creativity of Contemporary American Playwrights
abstract: About 250 years have passed since the Declaration of Independence.During the period, so many social and cultural ideologies and philosophies have been sophisticated and continued to influence upon American culture.Likewise, American drama has been also affected by such cultural and social conditions.Furthermore, the trend of literary critique evidently shows us that taking cultural and social conditions into consideration, many critics tend to regard American drama as the mirror of each temporality.However, there seem to be few studies that attempt to discover one of the characteristics of American drama as a whole.Therefore, this doctorial thesis attempts to find out one of the characteristics of American drama, through the chronological analysis of American drama from the early years of the republic all the way up to the present day.The first chapter explores James Nelson Barker s (1808) and Robert Montgomery Bird s (1831), in which two well-known characters in the American entertainment industry: Pocahontas and Spartacus were dramatized for the first time.Through the analysis of the manner of representation of these two characters, the issue of how the young republic established their personal and national identity through drama will be discussed.Adopting the Genesis and romanticizing America enabled some playwrights to represent American as a metaphysical divine nation.However, remarkable rationalization of science, historiography, and geology, which was based on the Enlightenment, ironically revealed its absence.Nonetheless, many stories that depict the encounter between primitiveness and civilization, adoration for primitiveness, and also the worship from primitiveness have been still produced.The reason of this phenomenon is that America is compelled to rely on fictionality derived from the literary imagination in order to preserve the basis of American identity.The second chapter describes Thornton Wilder, who is thought to be the same level as the father of American drama Eugene O Neil, and his 1931) and 1942).From meta-critical point of view, the manner of justification of American imperialism will be discussed.Although Wilder placed America within the great historical context, he attempted to universalize some motives as American originals.Consequently, we will discover that such a mechanism of universalization has something in common with theatrics.Furthermore, we will find out that representing America as a metaphysical divine nation is deeply connected to the expansion of American Imperialism.Additionally, our analysis reveals the inevitable conflict about peace that has resulted from contemporary American hegemony.In the third chapter, we shift our focus on a work written in the time when some playwrights could explore the notion of the self more freely than ever before.Through the analysis of ( 1959), one of the most distinguished American icons Tennessee Williams, his artistry mainly based on Neoclassicism, and his manner of self-representation will be discussed here.Although his manner of self-representation is so exclusive, egoistic, and narcissistic that some would feel utterly disgusted, such exclusiveness ironically encourages the current entertainment industry to highly flourish in contemporary America.His self-representation can be enabled with the vast amount of social, cultural, ant artistic legacies.However, those who live in America tend to forget the existence of the great legacies and consume a forged Williams as American icon.The fourth chapter discusses another prominent American playwright Sam Shepard, who has always explored himself in his art and one of his plays (1995).At the current time in which grand narratives have already collapsed, what course will American identity take?It is this profound issue that Shepard has ever grappled with in his drama.His literary imagination largely associated with modern technologies reveal how to establish and pursue postmodern identity.His exploration indicates a highly postmodern reality: he cannot depict their true selves but create their ideal selves.Even though Shepard notices that he can never be free from a huge influence of the past, his exploration paradoxically results in the drifting self in postmodern America.The influential past, so to speak, has become just another motive to explore one of the characteristics of contemporary America, namely, postmodernism.The last chapter describes a struggling playwright in postmodern America who eagerly longed for restructuring social and cultural formation through the creation of art.Through the analysis of August Wilson, one of the most prominent African American playwrights, his Pittsburgh Cycle, and his theatrical creativity, we discover that his manner of playwriting unveils his lifelong concern: what is art?Subsequently, his artistry helps us place American drama within the network of art, inherited from classical antiquity.The purpose of his art is to restore the aura that has vanished away from the traditional art.In other words, he attempted to reconstruct American culture with his Pittsburgh cycle as the central factor.However, this indicates that even Wilson, who had the most sincere attitude toward American culture, utilized the potential power of traditional art to establish Americanness.It can be reasonably said that he unconsciously Americanized the traditional art in creating his own art.As a consequence of the chronological analysis of American drama from the early years of the republic all the way up until the present day, we can surely define one of the characteristics of American drama.It is cultural imperialistic dynamics that support the basis of American drama, whether playwrights are conscious or unconscious of this phenomenon.Needless to say, it is characterized by adoption, romanticization, and Americanization of the cultural and historical legacies.

title: In This Issue
abstract: In A Bishop of Two Peoples: William of St. Calais and the Hybridization of Architecture in Eleventh-Century Durham, Meg Bernstein considers England's Durham Cathedral alongside the nearly contemporaneous Norman Chapel, located in the bishop's palace adjacent to the cathedral. Both were commissioned by Bishop William of St. Calais, the second Norman-appointed bishop of Durham. Bernstein argues that the dramatically different formal styles of the two buildings reflect politically motivated choices the bishop made following the Norman cultural conquest of England after 1066. While the cathedral is recognizably hybrid, recalling Anglo-Saxon formal motifs applied to a Norman plan, the castle chapel draws straight from the milieu of the duchy of Normandy. In particular, the chapel's stone capitals were most likely made in Normandy and brought to England by the bishop. This article seeks to provide context for the cathedral where it has been lost and to draw conclusions about the chapel's commission within the context of the Norman colonization of England.In Stone-Heng Restored (1655), Inigo Jones, the father of English neoclassicism, used drawings, histories, and questionable logic to argue that Stonehenge was built by the ancient Romans and that it originally exhibited perfect Platonic geometries. This argument was never given much credence, but by 1725 the subject matter and the architect had received enough attention that two book-length responses (a challenge and a defense) were published, and both were then republished in a single volume alongside Jones's original text. While most Jones scholars have neglected this work because of its logical and historical shortcomings, Ryan Roark argues in “Stonehenge in the Mind” and “Stonehenge on the Ground”: Reader, Viewer, and Object in Inigo Jones's Stone-Heng Restored (1655) that it was in fact exemplary of what made Jones, for many, a protomodern architect and scholar. Rather than viewing Jones's book as an earnest attempt to prove a historical inaccuracy, Roark considers it as an exercise in formal analysis, one that set the precedent for the contemporary pedagogical trend of using geometric simplifications of existing structures as a first step in new design. Jones's idiosyncratic reading of Stonehenge belied the idea that such analysis could be anything but intensely reliant on the subjectivity of both architect and viewer.In The Larkin's Technologies of Trust, Zeynep Çelik Alexander uses the card ledger invented by Darwin D. Martin, corporate secretary for the Larkin Company, as a starting point for a new history of a well-known modernist building: the Larkin Administration Building in Buffalo, New York, designed by Frank Lloyd Wright. Founded in 1875 as a soap manufacturer, the Larkin Company had grown dramatically by the beginning of the twentieth century, in large part because of innovative marketing strategies made possible by ingenious information-processing techniques. But it was also thanks to Wright's designs for office equipment—informed by principles of modularity and interchangeability—that armies of “human computers” were able to maintain this information regime. Çelik Alexander argues that the bureaucracy made possible by the Larkin Administration Building's architecture has been a blind spot in historiography; she aims to offer an architecturally oriented account of the history of data as epistemic unit, contending that the Larkin's protodatabase was, first and foremost, a moral technology predicated on managing networks of trust.In 1926, the remains of Siam's last absolute monarch were cremated on Bangkok's royal parade grounds, Sanam Luang, in a highly decorated ceremonial pyre known as the phra merumat or phra men. Modeled on Mount Meru, the center of the Vedic and Buddhist cosmos, ephemeral structures like this drew on the Traiphum phra ruang, a fourteenth-century text that elaborated the hierarchical structure of the universe and the exalted place of royalty within it. After the overthrow of the absolute monarchy in 1932, the sanctity of Sanam Luang was challenged when a controversial crematorium for commoners who died defending Siam's nascent constitution was built in the area once reserved for royalty. Together, the two crematoria played an important role in representing new forms of national belonging in the twentieth century that were consistent with older conceptions of social hierarchy. In A Tale of Two Crematoria: Funeral Architecture and the Politics of Representation in Mid-Twentieth-Century Bangkok, Lawrence Chua examines literary, pictorial, and architectural representations of the monumental crematoria from which powerful, meritorious people were historically dispatched to the upper echelons of the cosmos. As seen in seventeenth- and eighteenth-century temple murals and literature, the phra men was historically depicted as a space in which diverse social groups were brought together but hierarchically segregated. By the twentieth century, the above-noted crematoria for king and commoners—although radically different in appearance and ideology—could be understood as complementary structures that allowed older spatial and political approaches not only to survive but also to flourish in an era of turbulent social upheaval. Key to this continuity was the deployment of new modes of architectural representation such as the plan and section. Associated with Siam's nascent architectural profession and the rational representation of space, these tools depicted a modern form of political community and premodern social hierarchy while underscoring the shared fate of citizens and the state.Joanna C. Diman (1901–91): A “Cantankerous” Landscape Architect at Skidmore, Owings & Merrill presents a biographical overview of Diman's career as a landscape architect. Using hitherto unpublished sources, Nicholas Adams traces Diman's progress from her training at the Lowthorpe School of Landscape Architecture for Women (from which she graduated in 1923) through her early work for individual practitioners. For a decade beginning in 1934, she worked for the New York City Department of Parks. In 1944, she joined the New York office of Skidmore, Owings & Merrill, where she worked until her retirement in 1967. Archival sources at SOM reveal that she was involved to differing degrees in nearly all projects that passed through the firm's New York office, from the relatively small garden at Lever House to the great works of “pastoral capitalism,” such as that at Connecticut General in Bloomfield, Connecticut (1957). Adams raises questions of stylistic individuality and places them alongside the larger issue of what influence an in-house landscape department had on design at SOM during these years.

title: KOTTMAN, PAUL A., ed. The Insistence of Art: Aesthetic Philosophy after Early Modernity. Fordham University Press, 2017, vi + 298 pp., 26 b&w illus., $35.00 paper.
abstract: The Insistence of Art: Aesthetic Philosophy after Early Modernity, edited by Paul A. Kottman, reconsiders the importance of early modern artistic practices (from the Renaissance to the end of the Baroque) to our current understanding of both the historical development of aesthetics and the value of artistic practice and innovation to being themselves as subjects for philosophical discourse. In doing so, this collection of essays questions a number of “potted histories” with which we are culturally brought up whenever we think about the philosophy of aesthetics and its emergence as a branch of philosophy or inquiry in general. One such potted history is that it was not until the eighteenth century that an idea of the fine arts emerged and that notions of aesthetic autonomy were wholly the products of Enlightenment discourses, which originated from the realms of rationality and empiricism, ranging from Baumgarten to Hume. Indeed, one of the aims of this collection is to show how the ingredients for much Enlightenment discourse on aesthetics were already about, and indeed developed, during the early modern period. Moreover, this collection seeks to show how artistic practices themselves informed the aesthetic discourse of the early modern period. This is in stark contrast to the discourses on aesthetics that emerged in the early eighteenth century. According to Kottman, the theoretical engagement with aesthetics by eighteenth‐century theorists, to whom we normally attribute the emergence of aesthetic philosophy, had largely little to do with actual theories about art and more to do with how art, as an abstract principle, represented larger philosophical concepts. This is the second claim of this collection of essays: that “we find aesthetic philosophy's self‐articulation over the course of the eighteenth‐century and its introduction of an apparently new set of issues and questions for the human sciences” (p. 3). Kottman emphasizes that, while such discourses are valuable, they nevertheless ignore the philosophical value of distinct artistic practices and innovations within the artistic world. Third, the beginning of art history with J. J. Winkelmann's (1717–1768) study of art in antiquity and how it related to his contemporary neoclassical art world largely ignores, what this collection shows to be, the plethora of philosophically important artistic practices that emerged and evolved during the early modern period. Kottman argues that Winckelmann's approach of explaining the social world of antiquity through its artworks ignored, much like the eighteenth‐century theorists, the historical processes of artistic development. In contrast to Winckelmann stands Giorgio Vasari (1511–1574), who is also credited with writing the first history of art. Vasari sought to connect antiquity with the Florence of his day and to show a development of artistic practice. Winckelmann, on the contrary, ignored the early modern period which had largely fallen into distaste with the rise of neoclassicism and instead connected antiquity with his own epoch. This edition therefore attempts to rectify this imbalance, which has, at least partially, contributed to the exclusion of early modern artistic practices from aesthetic philosophy. The final aim of this collection is to problematize the periodization of the Renaissance and the Baroque as utterly distinct from other historical eras. Their isolation was a consequence of the advent of positivist historicism in the eighteenth century. Positivist historicism gave rise to the notion that one can uncover the “authentic” artwork through a piecing together of various facts about the author or the artwork while ignoring the artwork itself. Kottman argues that, “this work of returning to ‘original’ evidence of documents—and hence, of eliding the interpretations and revisions of intervening generations of artists and critiques—has deeply influenced the entrenchment of positivistic historicism as a dominant mode of humanist enquiry” (p. 14). Against this method stands the hermeneutical approach of figures, such as Herder, who, instead of holding Shakespeare at a distance in the cordoned‐off Renaissance brought him into the present, into the context of the eighteenth century. In the following four examples I hope to show how these aims are achieved to varying degrees. Victoria Kahn's essay, “Allegory, Poetic Theology, and Enlightenment Aesthetics,” focuses on the activity of reading allegorically as central to the conception of the autonomous aesthetic artifact in the early modern works of Marlowe's Doctor Faustus and Milton's Paradise Lost. Kahn's narrative follows a chronological development of reading allegorically beginning with Antiquity, through to Medieval Christianity and finishing with the Renaissance. “Poetic Theology” is first introduced as the activity of reading pagan myths allegorically. The necessity for such allegorical reading arose as a means of preserving the value of these myths by claiming that the poets of Antiquity were also theologians, and so deeper spiritual truths lay embedded within their texts. However, the immediate problem with such a conception is that, if we are to ignore the literal reading of pagan myth, which is a real theology for the pagans, then what is to prevent us from discounting Scripture itself as merely myth? This tension met with renewed force in the form of Medieval Christian theologians, such as Aquinas, who tried to deal with the fact that Scripture itself contained figurative expressions. If both Scripture and pagan myth contain figurative expressions and the figures of pagan myth were allowed to be subjected to allegorical reading so as to reach the deeper spiritual truths of these myths, then could not Scripture itself be reduced to the status of fiction precisely because of its own figurative expressions? In contrast to the theologians were the medieval poets, such as Dante, who played with the tensions between allegory as a form of literary expression and allegory as a hidden cosmological truth, which gave their work greater authority than if it were simply secular poetry. Such is the situation that the Renaissance is faced with: how to make use of pagan myth in a meaningful way without undermining the primacy of Scripture in the process. Kahn now shifts the focus onto three figures whom she argues laid the theoretical groundwork for something like the autonomous aesthetic artifact: Boccaccio, Ficino, and Erasmus. What is fundamental to all three figures is their insistence that the reader of pagan myth must engage with the text allegorically and, moreover, must approach such a reading as an exercise so as to adequately extract the hidden truths of the texts. However, this is not enough. Ficino, a Neoplatonist, argued that just as we can recognize the divine within ourselves because of our soul, so too can we recognize the divine in our creations, whatever they may be. In this respect, the creative exercise of reading allegorically elevates the “material reality of the text to higher spiritual truths” (p. 41). Kahn ends her essay with a thoughtful criticism of Panofsky and Cassirer, who argue that the idea of an aesthetic form in the Renaissance can be seen as anticipating Kant's idea of form as purposive purposelessness. She argues that this is a misrepresentation of the Renaissance's idea of form since the autonomous artifact of the Renaissance would be more akin to Kant's idea of dependent beauty. Indeed, for the Renaissance the aesthetic form derived its autonomous power precisely from the purposive engagement of the reader, viewer, with the artwork. Jon R. Snyder's essay, “Strokes of Wit Theorizing Beauty in Baroque Italy,” focuses on the prominent figures Emanuele Tesauro and Marco Boschini, whose individual works stand tall in their attempts to defend the Baroque vision of the world against that of Classicism. Both of these figures followed the poet Giovan Battista Marino on the importance of “Wit” in the Baroque. However, Snyder's efforts to elucidate the Baroque struggle do not stop at painters and poets but extend to the “New Science.” A prominent figure of the New Science, Galileo, had discovered the unpredictable solar phenomenon of sunspots, or macchia in Italian. This word, “macchia,” symbolizing wildness, a blemish, something unknown, soon found its way into the vocabulary of seventeenth‐century artists and art theorists. Indeed, the zenith of macchia was to express spontaneity on the canvas: a formless brush stroke that seemed empty of intentionality. The radical nature of the macchia stood in stark contrast with classical ideas of nature as harmonious, an image of nature that was stained with the “discovery” sunspots. Tesauro's theory of wit is best expressed in his seminal Il Cannocchiale Aristotelico, where he writes of metaphor in poetry, with Marino in mind, as the creative act of bringing together two disparate objects before the perceiver with the result of enlarging their knowledge of them. In this respect, metaphor “pricks the mind of the listener, reader, or viewer, provoking a novel thought or perspective that fills the mind with wonder and delight” (p. 200). Such is the power of wit for the Baroque, for it does not appear solely in poetry but in painting as well. However, Tesauro devotes little time to painting in Il Cannocchiale Aristotelico. In response, Snyder “fills‐in” a theory of wit for painting, based on an analysis of the frontispiece of the work. The result of this analysis is to show us that through pictorial representation and not just through metaphor in poetry, Tesauro sees the work of wit in the form of the macchia as exemplifying Baroque virtues. Moreover, Tesauro goes one step further and utilizes the “discovery” of macchia in the sixteenth century for the Baroque vision of the world. Indeed, it is because the Baroque destabilized the harmonious, classical representation of nature in art that the New Science could use its own imaginative faculty to understand the sunspots as representing discord with the hitherto accepted image of stable, Aristotelian celestial mechanics. Boschini takes a slightly different approach. Boschini's La carta del navegar pitoresco takes the reader through a tour of Venice's past and present artistic accomplishments. The theme of Venice as the free state of diplomacy is fundamental to Boschini's praise of Venetian art since he sees that very political freedom as expressed within the paintings of Titian and Tintoretto. Indeed, these principles of freedom turn the city itself into an aesthetic creation symbolizing the freedom of Venice. Venice is the aesthetic mastering of stone and water; imagine the winding canals of Venice as brushstrokes against a canvas. This is the first great reversal: art no longer imitates nature, but rather nature attempts to imitate art. Nature is now subordinated to art. The freedom of the Venetian maniera is expressed in the macchia, which is an expression of ineffable energy and free brushwork, independent of form. Commenting on Tintoretto's the Miracle of Saint Mark, Snyder writes that “it celebrates its witty self‐reflexivity or aesthetic estrangement‐effect, which compels the viewer to see it as artifice as well as a mirror of nature, while insisting that the former has greater cultural weight than the latter” (p. 217). Paul A. Kottman's essay, “Art and Philosophy in Hegel and Shakespeare,” focuses on a formal similarity that he observes between the epilogues of Hegel's Lectures on Fine Art and that of Shakespeare's The Tempest as delivered by Prospero. Kottman's claim is that both epilogues are demonstrations of their own freedom and rationality in virtue of being able to bring their respective activities to a provisional close. Kottman substantiates his claim from Hegel's own account of the development of art and more broadly from Hegel's distinction between objective and subjective spirit. Kottman understands objective spirit as “the sphere of collectively deliberated reasons for doing things” and subjective spirit as “the way in which self‐conscious individuals are formed in relation to those social rules and norms” (p. 125). Philosophy and art, as elements of Absolute Spirit, are in some ways part of objective spirit insofar as they can install a set of norms into society but differ from it insofar as they are able to reflexively evaluate our practices and perhaps even transform them. Kottman's reading of the epilogues relies on this ability to reflexively evaluate our practices. Prospero's epilogue is usually read as Shakespeare's own reflection on his dramatic work. Indeed Kottman's analysis of the epilogue of The Tempest follows this tradition of thought. In this respect, Prospero/Shakespeare is concluding his activity of acting/being a playwright by asking the audience, in his capacity as both actor and playwright, if they enjoyed both his performance and his dramatic works as a whole. Hegel ends his Lectures on Fine Art with the same request of his students. Hegel imitates this move of Prospero/Shakespeare as both lecturer and philosopher as a means of signaling the end of his lectures on aesthetics in a way that accords with the ideas of Romantic art. How does this imitation bring a satisfactory conclusion to Hegel's Lectures? Kottman's interpretation is that Hegel's understanding of Romantic art as self‐determining means that for Hegel to successfully conclude his philosophy of fine art he must demonstrate, instead of simply asserting or stating, the self‐determination of the age of Romantic art. Indeed, Hegel reenacts the subjective freedom exhibited by Prospero precisely to demonstrate this subjective freedom. This is the ‘dramatic education,’ according to Kottman, that Hegel displays in his epilogue. By ending their respective activities with these epilogues Hegel/Prospero admit an ending to their own contributions to their respective fields of philosophy of art/acting and “that new possibilities within the practice, beyond either carrying on our stopping altogether, are now available in light of the historical vantage achieved in the epilogues” (p. 134). Lydia Goehr's essay, “‘All Art Constantly Aspires to the Condition of Music’—Except Music,” discusses the claim that music has often been thought of through the “condition” of music, instead of simply as an artistic practice. This is because, in her view, such a rendering of music is to the detriment of its status as one of the sister arts. The usual claim, according to Goehr, is that music struggled from the Renaissance up to the middle of the eighteenth century to be taken seriously as an art because of its nonrepresentational form and content. This eventually reversed in the nineteenth century as the “negativity” of music became its crowning feature, as the union of a metaphysical form and content. Throughout this paragone, particularly between painting and music, is the preference for music as a metaphysical ideal over the practice of creating music. Goehr offers a genealogy, stretching from Antiquity to the present day of how the understanding of music through this metaphysical condition, instead of as a historically developing artistic practice, has simultaneously meant that the condition of music has forever acted as an aspiration for the all the other arts to reach while the act of playing music was considered either the lowest form of art or not an art at all. Goehr's genealogy begins with the myth of Marsyas. She theorizes that the competition between Marsyas and Apollo depicts a moment in which the tension between music as condition and music as art is expressed. Marsyas's music wins over the praise of the people because Apollo's music, being of such heavenly tones, is inaudible to the human ear, whereas Marysas's so‐called pedestrian music gives them pleasure. For Goehr this myth represents the banishment of music to the metaphysical realm, music as a condition, as a representation of celestial principles such as Pythagorean universal harmony. Goehr states that “there was no umbrella concept of music that covered everything that we now count as music as an art to the exclusion of all else. There was, rather, an umbrella concept and condition of mousikē on which so much more than music as art could and did make a claim” (p. 150)—much like Socrates’ appeal to music in the Phaedo as a way of reaching a higher truth in philosophy. Turning to Titian's painting of the Flaying of Marsyas, Goehr analyses how the art of painting sought to reach metaphysical, or musical, heights by showing the transfiguring powers of music. By representing the transfiguration of music, painting aspires toward the higher, divine condition of music in a bid to prove its value as an art. Furthermore, by seeking to represent music's transfiguration, painting attempts to assert itself as superior to music by proving the practice of painting to be better than the practice of music. Such is the criticism that Goehr traces from Titian to the mid‐eighteenth century. Goehr then traces how the condition of music—which had for so long thrown the value of music as artistic practice into question but which gave the other arts something to aspire toward—gave it the status of an independent art. However, the fundamental problem remained: the condition of music was what elevated music above the other arts, and not the practice of music. Therefore, music continued to be talked of as spiritual or pure aesthetic form (á la Eduard Hanslick) instead of as a practice. Indeed, the only way the nineteenth century could validate the status of music as an art was to emphasize the metaphysical conception of it, to embrace its condition to the detriment of the art itself. The remaining six essays of this edition approach their problematics in much the same way as I have outlined in the above four reviews. Each essay contributes toward the aims as expressed in the beginning of the book. They do not attempt to supplant or even directly engage with eighteenth‐century theories of aesthetics. Instead, they problematize the generally accepted moment of aesthetic singularity that is the eighteenth century. Without discarding the variety of philosophies of aesthetics from Leibniz to Kant, they expand our horizons and show us, with a very Hegelian approach, the development of artistic practices, principles, and the aesthetic theories over history. Furthermore, true to their aims, they keep their arguments firmly within the domain of artists and art critics, carefully showing a way of philosophically discussing art that does not simply subsume art under a more general, grander even, concept of philosophy. Rather they show how art and philosophy are constantly in dialogue. This Hegelian approach, as demonstrated in Kottman's essay, of showing the development of practices as philosophically relevant in themselves is perhaps a path that should be followed in future dialogues between philosophy and art.

title: Notes on Writing as Vertigo
abstract: Detail from Gustave Flaubert, ‘Trois contes, La légende saint Julien Hospitalier’, 1875 (plate 1). Gustave Flaubert, manuscript page from ‘Trois contes, La légende saint Julien Hospitalier’, 1875. NAF 23663 (2), folio 429. Paris: Bibliothèque nationale de France (BnF). This essay began as an occasional response to two papers at the ‘Writing Art History’ conference from which this special issue emerged. I have maintained the informal and speculative tone of an address to an audience in this text. Why at this moment should we want to fuse creative writing and the discourse of art history, and to effect a contamination of genres? Perhaps it is because an obstinate and regressive ‘realist’ mode of art history writing still dominates our profession. The nominal authority of the artwork over our superficial secondary elaborations on it, responsibility or so-called fidelity to the work of art itself, and, tangentially, linguistic clarity and communicability as vehicles of a tyranny of common sense; these are the restrictive elements of an art-historical writing in a realist mode. If ‘language’, as Theodor W. Adorno claimed, ‘imprisons those who speak it’, reaching out to creative writing might yield a certain purchase on freedom.1 Therefore, efforts are being made to propel ourselves out of a realist discourse, and to write art history differently. We could raise objections to each of the realist presuppositions. The first – the ‘authority’ of the artwork – leads us to ignore the act of writing itself as generative of another quite autonomous discourse; the second assumes that writing art history proceeds as if involved in an act of translation, tethering and binding our language to the primary art object with the aim of fidelity (whereas a philosophical critique of translation renders the grounds of this presumption questionable); the third is ideological, insofar as ‘common sense’, or a certain type of communicative writing, is, it has been claimed, inimical to new, creative, thought.2 If an essential aspect of what we call modernity is a critical reflection on the act of writing, from Mallarmé to Proust to Joyce, one way of thinking ourselves out of a realist art history would involve recourse to some great and critical thinkers of modernity, outside the constricting bounds of art history.3 And not only in literature, but also philosophy: the names, variously, of Kant, Hegel, Bataille, Derrida, and Barthes were raised in the Writing Art History project.4 Other more utopian gestures of imagining an art history writing would accede to the free play of the fictional, flirt with the surreal, submit to the anecdotal, or begin to poeticize our professional discourse. To explore these thoughts further, I want to turn to two writers who span the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, formative of modernity and its critical relation to writing. First, a nineteenth-century novelist who is indeed synonymous with the act of writing, that ‘homme-plume’ Gustave Flaubert. Second, a twentieth-century cultural critic and philosopher who was no less a great stylist; and who crucially and critically reflected on the possibilities of writing ‘poetically’ in conditions of modernity, Theodor W. Adorno. Their praxis and conceptions about writing might be instructive when reflecting upon the expanding possibilities of writing art history now. Both apprehended the act of writing with a high degree of urgency and self-criticism, both struggled to write poetically (we will see how much). At this moment when art-historical discourse wishes to flirt, or couple with, creative writing, let us bring art history’s discourse into a critical relation to creative writing. This means first of all to admit that we are not in control: that the act of writing creatively involves for the writer aporia, nausea, and vertigo. These two writers’ sovereign command of their writing, and their presumed self-abstention from their literary works, may appear old-fashioned, but what I want to draw attention to is their vertiginous subjectivity in producing the most perfect of written works. In order to speak of Flaubert’s writing practice I will turn to Roland Barthes. But for me it is a very particular Barthes. I turn to Barthes as a writer who thinks now not about the great critical project of post-structuralism, or about the notional shift from the ‘readerly’ to the ‘writerly’ text; or even about mounting a critique of the ‘reality effect’ of historical narrative discourse, but simply about the act of writing as such, and particularly about writing as a way of life.5 This is the Barthes of the little essay that he wrote in 1967, entitled ‘Flaubert and the Sentence’.6 That essay brings together the subject of writing and the nineteenth-century artwork.7 Why I turn to this Barthes, rather than, say, to the Barthes of ‘The Discourse of History’– which would be a more obvious lead into a thinking about Art History as a discourse – is because in the 1967 essay Barthes addresses the process of writing in its smallest, minutest, and most discrete form: that of changing a sentence, and re-changing, and changing it again and again. And with Flaubert as his producing subject – artist, if you like – he thinks and indeed empathizes about the affect of all this activity, about how writing feels.8 But it is also because I encountered the essay with an immediate recognition, which explained my long discomfort with professional art history writing – and actually with writing at all, for I panic before a blank postcard. ‘Flaubert and the Sentence’ began to make sense of the existential experience of writing in its more heightened manifestations as one which inexorably approaches the dizzying condition of nausea, or the sensation of vertigo. This is to turn the question of ‘Writing Art History’ to its more intimate manifestations: not to the grand systems or anti-systems of Hegel, or Kant, or Bataille, and not to the impossible dilemma of the inexpressible, or non-reason, but to the mechanics of the articulated, the must-be-expressed as produced by a particular subjectivity undergoing a crisis of writing. The 1967 Barthes essay expertly discloses the inexorable logic of that state or stasis of writing, as a textual operation produced by a suffering subject. Excluding for the moment all the other business of the professional art historian, what essentially is creative writing like as a way of life? For Flaubert, as presented by Barthes, writing is an unending, intolerable process that is never given to meet its object in any naïve sense (its object being for Flaubert ‘reality’, and for the art historian, the artwork). Why does Flaubert write? Not for the deadline, or for the publisher, but simply for itself: ‘writing [for Flaubert] is the book’s goal, not publication’, says Barthes.9 What Flaubert practices is a kind of ‘pure writing’. But this is not to say it is free – although it is free from functionality, and from external peer pressure – or rather it does not mean that Flaubert experiences writing as freedom. In fact, it is atrocious. For Flaubert, ‘writing is absolute suffering, useless suffering. Writing is disproportionately slow (‘four pages this week’, ‘five days for a page’, ‘two days to reach the end of two lines’.)10 He throws himself on a couch to recover. ‘Sometimes’, Flaubert says (1852), ‘when I feel empty, when expression is refractory, when after having scribbled many pages I discover I haven’t made a single sentence, I fall on my couch and lie there stupefied in an inner marsh of ennui.’11 And the recovery – on the couch (and yet before Freud) – never comes, just a vertigo of desperation. In 1875, the cry ‘I have spent my life depriving my heart of its most legitimate nourishment; I have led a laborious and austere existence. And now I can bear no more, I am at the end of my tether.’12 Barthes de-romanticizes what we may think of blandly as the all too familiar complaints of the nineteenth-century artist, by proceeding to describe what Flaubert is actually doing during all those desperate and austere years. He complicates the notion of Flaubert as a highly controlled perfectionist and a cold stylist by exposing the irrational aspects of making a perfect sentence, the madness that is inherent in it. Flaubert is making substitutions, or ‘substitutive corrections’ on his manuscripts, or what Barthes calls ‘the vertigo of an infinite correction’: crossing out one word for another, another for another, another for another, agonizingly, interminably (plate 1).13 For sure, there is a full stop, a ‘fin’, and an end to this all – and indeed the works do get published – but the finishing, this publication, is a derisory and hardly compensatory incidental fact. The process of writing, Flaubert’s ‘life’ (of which he himself is increasingly contemptuous) is not one of possession and completion – of producing a finely formed canon – but of endless substitutive work.14 For Flaubert, writing ‘for a living’– and this is the irony – becomes a life sacrificed to the operation of substitution. Stupefaction, vertigo. This implies that one way to write art history differently may be less variously to incorporate a novelistic mode, or to ‘modernize’, or ‘postmodernize’ our textuality, in a more or less programmatic way, than to effect minute substitutions. What would it mean simply to substitute the word Duchamp for Degas, or Ghirlandaio for Gauguin? It would not only set in place a vast out-of-time-ness – delicious and perplexing anachronicity of senseless, or differently sense-producing gestures – it would also unfix our art-historical careers and the names to which we tether ourselves, and for which we are known to each other, it would deliver us onto uncontrollable and unimagined terrains. Substitutions – substitutability – this would really shake up art history, and through the process itself of writing (understood as the vertigo, not the play but the nausea, of substitutions). Of course, they will never let us do it, for the sake of the profession, the disciplining all-importance of peer review to which Flaubert could be blind, and imperatives of historical responsibility. If the binding community that ‘names’– including a professional art history community (and we have not yet attained an art history without names) – is constituted and transmitted through a tacit and repeatedly enacted agreement to exclude a certain type of substitution, misnaming, or the queer catachrestic, then it has the power of a radical risk to order.15 And, given Flaubert’s suffering, we may anyway not wish to take the risk. Should one remain faithful to the names of art history? If, for example, a dedicated art-historical writing follows the pulse of the artwork, or its method, as if mimetically, what would be the consequence of my moving from writing about Jacques-Louis David’s neoclassicism to that of Cy Twombly’s lapsed and decentred abstract expressionism? The one involves all neoclassical reiteration and careful substitutive work and the other delicious and dangerous lassitude of the classical sentence.16 And yet caught up only in the cadence of my sentences, I do not wish to imitate David’s monumentalizing attitude to the sentence – reified, rigid words inscribed there in the painted surfaces of his canvases – and in my writing of a sentence I still come closer to the sickening vertigo of a Flaubert than to the beautiful lassitude of a Twombly. Our contemporary concern for the piecemeal, the fragmentary, and the chronically incomplete, if not the erased, discloses Flaubert’s obsession with the work of substitution as peculiarly modern. The mania for substitution, its chronic lingering over detail, is a symptom of the impossibility of writing propulsive narrative history; and the nineteenth-century moment suggestively coincides with the inauguration of professional art history writing. It is here that one might want to touch on the most ambitious of nineteenth-century constructors of pseudo-historical narrative, who yet could find it impossible to tell a simple story. Or, rather, whose work stages a symptomatic tension between the will to grand narrative (but actual failure of diachronic impulse) and the reality of the piecemeal and repetitive fragment (improper obsession with the synchronic impulse and ‘proper’ substitutions). This is the figure of Richard Wagner, the magician-procurer of the ‘total work of art’, master of writing. For it has often occurred to me to wonder why I simply cannot remember the story of Wagner’s Götterdammerung, the last of the Ring cycle, having seen it at least four times (once in total immersion and purposeful lack of distraction in Bayreuth, 2001), and listened to it on recordings now countless times. Listening to it, or recalling Wagner’s immense narrative opera, I can remember the next note – or constellation of notes – and the next and the next, almost perfectly. But what is every time lost to me is what is happening, or about to happen, in the narrative. As a piece of grand narrative history, and in spite of Wagner’s total control of text, music, and image in his lifetime, there is a curious disjuncture between narrative progression and musical picture. This is not just my usual terrible memory for a plot – or for the argument of an academic article – it is something Wagner the composer and writer is surely aware of, and keeps trying to compensate for. It is immanent to the work. What else makes Wagner operas so very long, if not the stopping of the narrative again and again to recapitulate, to retell the story; right from the beginning three operas back where the Rhine maidens gather: to spend another half hour telling what has happened over the last three hours. For Adorno, Wagner desperately writes towards new totalities – which have, however, been lost. Flaubert immersed himself in the process of substitution and was left only with a heightened affect of stupefaction. Wagner’s open admission to the impossibility of writing historical narrative in the nineteenth century stupefies us, the audience, through the opera’s extraordinary, compelling, and exhausting length and stopping of time and space; although, as Adrian Rifkin reminds us, there is always the possibility that ‘the performance itself is not only a realizing, a transformation of narrative or interpretative perspective, but an alteration that occurs in a separate space from the musicology of the score as such, and transforms it.’17 Which leads us to the question, of the experience of the audience for, or reception, of writing. For if, as Adorno pointed out, in Wagner’s case the audience is accosted, violently attacked through a sort of musical pulverization, a similar authoritarian style should not be adopted by the art historian writer of today, as a symptom of and alibi for the experiential agonies and real exhaustion of grand narratives which have been the condition of writing since the nineteenth century, and which continue to haunt us. The case of Wagner shows us how a new kind of writing – or in this case composing – might stupefy the listener, or ‘writerly’ reader, through the battles waged within the work of art against the threat of aporia (Wagner’s work is full of falsely triumphant closures, and the arresting of time and of the propulsion of narrative produce a synchronic and substitutive mythic space). It also demonstrates how self-declarative and highly ambitious poetic writing might be compromised by the very pragmatic functionalities that it seeks to transcend. And so it is with Adorno, and his critical reflections upon the condition of writing in modernity, that I will end: what are the larger forces that might be at play in this move from a communicative writing to a more poetic one? Adorno sees a tension, which he traces back to the nineteenth century, between the two kinds of writing, the poetic and the communicative.18 The poetic is the domain of expressive language, the communicative that of pragmatic; if the latter is the purposeful and determinant language of both governmentality and market forces (capitalism), the former, for Adorno, approaches the condition of music (he uses the term ‘rustling’ to describe this kind of language act, as does Barthes, later19 ).
